connect.title: Spark Connect
connect.blurb: The client/server protocol: thin clients in any language talk gRPC to a Spark server.

streaming.title: Structured Streaming
streaming.blurb: Incremental processing, state, triggers and the real-time mode.

pipelines.title: Declarative Pipelines
pipelines.blurb: Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP): datasets and flows declared in SQL or Python, run as a graph.

types.title: Data types
types.blurb: Types beyond the classics: variant, time, geospatial, collated strings.

semantics.title: Semantic layer
semantics.blurb: Metric views and other ways to define business logic once.

python.title: PySpark
python.blurb: Python APIs, UDFs, Arrow and Python-defined data sources.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.blurb: Formats and connectors that ship with Spark.

execution.title: Execution and performance
execution.blurb: How queries run: adaptive execution, caching, scheduling.

ops.title: Operations
ops.blurb: Logging, UI, deployment and the runtime platform.

ml.title: Machine learning
ml.blurb: Spark ML, including ML over Spark Connect.

platform.title: Platform capabilities
platform.blurb: What the vendor adds around Spark: table formats, native engines, GPUs. Vendor-documented only.

function.name: aggregate
function.usage:
aggregate(expr, start, merge, finish) - Applies a binary operator to an initial state and all
elements in the array, and reduces this to a single state. The final state is converted
into the final result by applying a finish function.

function.name: array_contains
function.usage: array_contains(array, value) - Returns true if the array contains the value, false if not. Returns null if the array or value is null, or if the value is not found and the array contains a null element.

function.name: array_distinct
function.usage: array_distinct(array) - Removes duplicate values from the array.

function.name: array_except
function.usage:
array_except(array1, array2) - Returns an array of the elements in array1 but not in array2,
without duplicates.

function.name: exists
function.usage: exists(expr, pred) - Tests whether a predicate holds for one or more elements in the array.

function.name: filter
function.usage: filter(expr, func) - Filters the input array using the given predicate.

function.name: forall
function.usage: forall(expr, pred) - Tests whether a predicate holds for all elements in the array.

function.name: array_intersect
function.usage:
array_intersect(array1, array2) - Returns an array of the elements in the intersection of array1 and

function.name: array_join
function.usage:
array_join(array, delimiter[, nullReplacement]) - Concatenates the elements of the given array

function.name: array_max
function.usage:
array_max(array) - Returns the maximum value in the array. NaN is greater than
any non-NaN elements for double/float type. NULL elements are skipped.

function.name: array_min
function.usage:
array_min(array) - Returns the minimum value in the array. NaN is greater than
any non-NaN elements for double/float type. NULL elements are skipped.

function.name: array_position
function.usage:
array_position(array, element) - Returns the (1-based) index of the first matching element of
the array as long, or 0 if no match is found.

function.name: array_remove
function.usage: array_remove(array, element) - Remove all elements that equal to element from array.

function.name: array_repeat
function.usage: array_repeat(element, count) - Returns the array containing element count times.

function.name: array_sort
function.example: SELECT array_sort(array(5, 6, 1), (left, right) -> case when left < right then -1 when left > right then 1 else 0 end)
function.usage:
array_sort(expr, func) - Sorts the input array. If func is omitted, sort
in ascending order. The elements of the input array must be orderable.
NaN is greater than any non-NaN elements for double/float type.
Null elements will be placed at the end of the returned array.
Since 3.0.0 this function also sorts and returns the array based on the
given comparator function. The comparator will take two arguments representing
two elements of the array.
It returns a negative integer, 0, or a positive integer as the first element is less than,
equal to, or greater than the second element. If the comparator function returns null,
the function will fail and raise an error.

function.name: arrays_zip

function.name: current_database

function.name: current_date
function.usage:
current_date() - Returns the current date at the start of query evaluation. All calls of current_date within the same query return the same value.
current_date - Returns the current date at the start of query evaluation.

function.name: current_timestamp
function.usage:
current_timestamp() - Returns the current timestamp at the start of query evaluation. All calls of current_timestamp within the same query return the same value.
current_timestamp - Returns the current timestamp at the start of query evaluation.
current_timestamp(precision) - Returns the current timestamp at the start of query evaluation, with the given fractional-seconds precision. A precision in [7, 9] returns a nanosecond-precision TIMESTAMP_LTZ(precision) and requires spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled to be true; precision 6 returns the standard microsecond TIMESTAMP.

function.name: date_sub

function.name: dayofyear

function.name: decode
function.usage:
decode(bin, charset) - Decodes the first argument using the second argument character set. If either argument is null, the result will also be null.
decode(expr, search, result [, search, result ] ... [, default]) - Compares expr
to each search value in order. If expr is equal to a search value, decode returns
the corresponding result. If no match is found, then it returns default. If default
is omitted, it returns null.

function.name: dense_rank
function.example: SELECT a, b, dense_rank(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
dense_rank() - Computes the rank of a value in a group of values. The result is one plus the
previously assigned rank value. Unlike the function rank, dense_rank will not produce gaps
in the ranking sequence.
expr1 / expr2 - Returns `expr1`/`expr2`. It always performs floating point division.

function.name: element_at
function.usage:
element_at(array, index) - Returns element of array at given (1-based) index. If Index is 0,
Spark will throw an error. If index < 0, accesses elements from the last to the first.
The function returns NULL if the index exceeds the length of the array and
`spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is set to false.
If `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is set to true, it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
for invalid indices.
element_at(map, key) - Returns value for given key. The function returns NULL if the key is not
contained in the map.

function.name: elt
function.usage:
elt(n, input1, input2, ...) - Returns the `n`-th input, e.g., returns `input2` when `n` is 2.
The function returns NULL if the index exceeds the length of the array
and `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is set to false. If `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is set to true,
it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for invalid indices.

function.name: encode
function.usage: encode(str, charset) - Encodes the first argument using the second argument character set. If either argument is null, the result will also be null.

expr1 <=> expr2 - Returns same result as the EQUAL(=) operator for non-null operands,
but returns true if both are null, false if one of the them is null.
expr1 = expr2 - Returns true if `expr1` equals `expr2`, or false otherwise.
expr1 == expr2 - Returns true if `expr1` equals `expr2`, or false otherwise.

function.name: e
function.usage: e() - Returns Euler's number, e.

function.name: exp
function.usage: exp(expr) - Returns e to the power of `expr`.

function.name: explode
function.usage: explode(expr) - Separates the elements of array `expr` into multiple rows, or the elements of map `expr` into multiple rows and columns. Unless specified otherwise, uses the default column name `col` for elements of the array or `key` and `value` for the elements of the map.

function.name: explode_outer
function.usage: explode_outer(expr) - Separates the elements of array `expr` into multiple rows, or the elements of map `expr` into multiple rows and columns. Unless specified otherwise, uses the default column name `col` for elements of the array or `key` and `value` for the elements of the map.

function.name: expm1
function.usage: expm1(expr) - Returns exp(`expr`) - 1.

function.name: extract
function.usage: extract(field FROM source) - Extracts a part of the date or timestamp or time or interval source.

function.name: factorial
function.usage: factorial(expr) - Returns the factorial of `expr`. `expr` is [0..20]. Otherwise, null.

function.name: find_in_set
function.usage:
find_in_set(str, str_array) - Returns the index (1-based) of the given string (`str`) in the comma-delimited list (`str_array`).
Returns 0, if the string was not found or if the given string (`str`) contains a comma.

function.name: flatten
function.usage: flatten(arrayOfArrays) - Transforms an array of arrays into a single array.

function.name: floor
function.usage: floor(expr[, scale]) - Returns the largest number after rounding down that is not greater than `expr`. An optional `scale` parameter can be specified to control the rounding behavior.

function.name: format_number
function.usage:
format_number(expr1, expr2) - Formats the number `expr1` like '#,###,###.##', rounded to `expr2`
decimal places. If `expr2` is 0, the result has no decimal point or fractional part.
`expr2` also accept a user specified format.
This is supposed to function like MySQL's FORMAT.

function.name: format_string

function.name: from_utc_timestamp
function.usage: from_utc_timestamp(timestamp, timezone) - Given a timestamp like '2017-07-14 02:40:00.0', interprets it as a time in UTC, and renders that time as a timestamp in the given time zone. For example, 'GMT+1' would yield '2017-07-14 03:40:00.0'.

function.name: from_unixtime
function.usage: from_unixtime(unix_time[, fmt]) - Returns `unix_time` in the specified `fmt`.

function.name: get_json_object
function.usage: get_json_object(json_txt, path) - Extracts a json object from `path`.
expr1 > expr2 - Returns true if `expr1` is greater than `expr2`.

function.name: grouping
function.example: SELECT name, grouping(name), sum(age) FROM VALUES (2, 'Alice'), (5, 'Bob') people(age, name) GROUP BY cube(name)
function.usage:
grouping(col) - indicates whether a specified column in a GROUP BY is aggregated or
not, returns 1 for aggregated or 0 for not aggregated in the result set.",

function.name: grouping_id
function.example: SELECT name, grouping_id(), sum(age), avg(height) FROM VALUES (2, 'Alice', 165), (5, 'Bob', 180) people(age, name, height) GROUP BY cube(name, height)

grouping_id([col1[, col2 ..]]) - returns the level of grouping, equals to

function.name: hex
function.usage: hex(expr) - Converts `expr` to hexadecimal.

function.name: hour
function.usage:
hour(expr) - Returns the hour component of the given expression.
If `expr` is a TIMESTAMP or a string that can be cast to timestamp,
it returns the hour of that timestamp.
If `expr` is a nanosecond-precision timestamp TIMESTAMP_NTZ(p) or TIMESTAMP_LTZ(p)
with p in [7, 9] (since 4.3.0), it returns the hour of that timestamp, ignoring the
sub-microsecond digits.
If `expr` is a TIME type (since 4.1.0), it returns the hour of the time-of-day.

function.name: ifnull

initcap(str) - Returns `str` with the first letter of each word in uppercase.

function.name: inline_outer

function.name: json_tuple
function.usage: json_tuple(jsonStr, p1, p2, ..., pn) - Returns a tuple like the function get_json_object, but it takes multiple names. All the input parameters and output column types are string.

function.name: lag
function.example: SELECT a, b, lag(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
lag(input[, offset[, default]]) - Returns the value of `input` at the `offset`th row
before the current row in the window. The default value of `offset` is 1 and the default
value of `default` is null. If the value of `input` at the `offset`th row is null,
null is returned. If there is no such offset row (e.g., when the offset is 1, the first
row of the window does not have any previous row), `default` is returned.

function.name: last_day
function.usage: last_day(date) - Returns the last day of the month which the date belongs to.

function.name: lead
function.example: SELECT a, b, lead(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
lead(input[, offset[, default]]) - Returns the value of `input` at the `offset`th row
after the current row in the window. The default value of `offset` is 1 and the default
value of `default` is null. If the value of `input` at the `offset`th row is null,
null is returned. If there is no such an offset row (e.g., when the offset is 1, the last
row of the window does not have any subsequent row), `default` is returned.

function.name: make_timestamp
function.usage:
make_timestamp(year, month, day, hour, min, sec[, timezone]) - Create the current timestamp with local time zone from year, month, day, hour, min, sec and timezone fields. If the configuration `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is false, the function returns NULL on invalid inputs. Otherwise, it will throw an error instead.
make_timestamp(date[, time[, timezone]]) - Create timestamp from date and time fields.

function.name: map_concat
function.usage: map_concat(map, ...) - Returns the union of all the given maps

function.name: map_entries
function.usage: map_entries(map) - Returns an unordered array of all entries in the given map.

function.name: map_filter
function.usage: map_filter(expr, func) - Filters entries in a map using the function.

function.name: map_from_arrays
function.usage:
map_from_arrays(keys, values) - Creates a map with a pair of the given key/value arrays. All elements
in keys should not be null

function.name: map_from_entries
function.usage: map_from_entries(arrayOfEntries) - Returns a map created from the given array of entries.

function.name: map_keys
function.usage: map_keys(map) - Returns an unordered array containing the keys of the map.

function.name: map_values
function.usage: map_values(map) - Returns an unordered array containing the values of the map.

function.name: map_zip_with
function.example: SELECT map_zip_with(map(1, 'a', 2, 'b'), map(1, 'x', 2, 'y'), (k, v1, v2) -> concat(v1, v2))
function.usage:
map_zip_with(map1, map2, function) - Merges two given maps into a single map by applying
function to the pair of values with the same key. For keys only presented in one map,
NULL will be passed as the value for the missing key. If an input map contains duplicated
keys, only the first entry of the duplicated key is passed into the lambda function.

function.name: md5
function.usage: md5(expr) - Returns an MD5 128-bit checksum as a hex string of `expr`.

function.name: minute
function.usage:
minute(expr) - Returns the minute component of the given expression.
If `expr` is a TIMESTAMP or a string that can be cast to timestamp,
it returns the minute of that timestamp.
If `expr` is a nanosecond-precision timestamp TIMESTAMP_NTZ(p) or TIMESTAMP_LTZ(p)
with p in [7, 9] (since 4.3.0), it returns the minute of that timestamp, ignoring the
sub-microsecond digits.
If `expr` is a TIME type (since 4.1.0), it returns the minute of the time-of-day.

function.name: monotonically_increasing_id
function.usage:
monotonically_increasing_id() - Returns monotonically increasing 64-bit integers. The generated ID is guaranteed
to be monotonically increasing and unique, but not consecutive. The current implementation
puts the partition ID in the upper 31 bits, and the lower 33 bits represent the record number
within each partition. The assumption is that the data frame has less than 1 billion
partitions, and each partition has less than 8 billion records.
The function is non-deterministic because its result depends on partition IDs.

function.name: month
function.usage: month(date) - Returns the month component of the date/timestamp.

function.name: months_between
function.usage:
months_between(timestamp1, timestamp2[, roundOff]) - If `timestamp1` is later than `timestamp2`, then the result
is positive. If `timestamp1` and `timestamp2` are on the same day of month, or both
are the last day of month, time of day will be ignored. Otherwise, the difference is
calculated based on 31 days per month, and rounded to 8 digits unless roundOff=false.
expr1 * expr2 - Returns `expr1`*`expr2`.

function.name: hash
function.usage: hash(expr1, expr2, ...) - Returns a hash value of the arguments.

function.name: ntile
function.example: SELECT a, b, ntile(2) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
ntile(n) - Divides the rows for each window partition into `n` buckets ranging
from 1 to at most `n`.

function.name: nanvl
function.usage: nanvl(expr1, expr2) - Returns `expr1` if it's not NaN, or `expr2` otherwise.

function.name: next_day
function.usage:
next_day(start_date, day_of_week) - Returns the first date which is later than `start_date` and named as indicated.
The function returns NULL if at least one of the input parameters is NULL.
When both of the input parameters are not NULL and day_of_week is an invalid input,
the function throws SparkIllegalArgumentException if `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is set to true, otherwise NULL.
! expr - Logical not.

function.name: not
function.usage: not expr - Logical not.

function.name: now
function.usage:
now() - Returns the current timestamp at the start of query evaluation. All calls of now within the same query return the same value.
now(precision) - Returns the current timestamp at the start of query evaluation, with the given fractional-seconds precision. A precision in [7, 9] returns a nanosecond-precision TIMESTAMP_LTZ(precision) and requires spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled to be true; precision 6 returns the standard microsecond TIMESTAMP.

function.name: nullif
function.usage: nullif(expr1, expr2) - Returns null if `expr1` equals to `expr2`, or `expr1` otherwise.

function.name: nvl
function.usage: nvl(expr1, expr2) - Returns `expr2` if `expr1` is null, or `expr1` otherwise.

function.name: nvl2
function.usage: nvl2(expr1, expr2, expr3) - Returns `expr2` if `expr1` is not null, or `expr3` otherwise.

function.name: octet_length
function.usage: octet_length(expr) - Returns the byte length of string data or number of bytes of binary

function.name: or
function.usage: expr1 or expr2 - Logical OR.

function.name: overlay
function.usage: overlay(input, replace, pos[, len]) - Replace `input` with `replace` that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`.

function.name: to_date
function.usage:
to_date(date_str[, fmt]) - Parses the `date_str` expression with the `fmt` expression to
a date. Returns null with invalid input. By default, it follows casting rules to a date if
the `fmt` is omitted.

function.name: to_timestamp
function.usage:
to_timestamp(timestamp_str[, fmt]) - Parses the `timestamp_str` expression with the `fmt` expression
to a timestamp. Returns null with invalid input. By default, it follows casting rules to
a timestamp if the `fmt` is omitted. The result data type is consistent with the value of
configuration `spark.sql.timestampType`.

function.name: parse_url
function.usage: parse_url(url, partToExtract[, key]) - Extracts a part from a URL.

function.name: percent_rank
function.example: SELECT a, b, percent_rank(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage: percent_rank() - Computes the percentage ranking of a value in a group of values.

function.name: pi
function.usage: pi() - Returns pi.

function.name: pmod
function.usage: pmod(expr1, expr2) - Returns the positive value of `expr1` mod `expr2`.

function.name: posexplode_outer
function.usage: posexplode_outer(expr) - Separates the elements of array `expr` into multiple rows with positions, or the elements of map `expr` into multiple rows and columns with positions. Unless specified otherwise, uses the column name `pos` for position, `col` for elements of the array or `key` and `value` for elements of the map.

function.name: posexplode
function.usage: posexplode(expr) - Separates the elements of array `expr` into multiple rows with positions, or the elements of map `expr` into multiple rows and columns with positions. Unless specified otherwise, uses the column name `pos` for position, `col` for elements of the array or `key` and `value` for elements of the map.

function.name: pow
function.usage: pow(expr1, expr2) - Raises `expr1` to the power of `expr2`.

function.name: power
function.usage: power(expr1, expr2) - Raises `expr1` to the power of `expr2`.

function.name: quarter
function.usage: quarter(date) - Returns the quarter of the year for date, in the range 1 to 4.

function.name: rlike
function.usage: rlike(str, regexp) - Returns true if `str` matches `regexp`, or false otherwise.

function.name: rank
function.example: SELECT a, b, rank(b) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
rank() - Computes the rank of a value in a group of values. The result is one plus the number
of rows preceding or equal to the current row in the ordering of the partition. The values
will produce gaps in the sequence.

function.name: regexp_extract
function.usage:
regexp_extract(str, regexp[, idx]) - Extract the first string in the `str` that match the `regexp`
expression and corresponding to the regex group index.

function.name: regexp_replace
function.usage: regexp_replace(str, regexp, rep[, position]) - Replaces all substrings of `str` that match `regexp` with `rep`.
expr1 % expr2, or mod(expr1, expr2) - Returns the remainder after `expr1`/`expr2`.

function.name: mod
function.usage: expr1 % expr2, or mod(expr1, expr2) - Returns the remainder after `expr1`/`expr2`.

function.name: reverse
function.usage:
reverse(expr) - Returns a reversed string, a binary value with bytes in reverse order,
or an array with reverse order of elements.

function.name: right
function.usage: right(str, len) - Returns the rightmost `len`(`len` can be string type) characters from the string `str`,if `len` is less or equal than 0 the result is an empty string.

function.name: rint
function.usage: rint(expr) - Returns the double value that is closest in value to the argument and is equal to a mathematical integer.

function.name: rollup
function.example: SELECT name, age, count(*) FROM VALUES (2, 'Alice'), (5, 'Bob') people(age, name) GROUP BY rollup(name, age)

function.name: round
function.usage: round(expr, d) - Returns `expr` rounded to `d` decimal places using HALF_UP rounding mode.

function.name: row_number
function.example: SELECT a, b, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
row_number() - Assigns a unique, sequential number to each row, starting with one,
according to the ordering of rows within the window partition.

function.name: schema_of_csv
function.usage: schema_of_csv(csv[, options]) - Returns schema in the DDL format of CSV string.

function.name: schema_of_json
function.usage: schema_of_json(json[, options]) - Returns schema in the DDL format of JSON string.

function.name: second
function.usage:
second(expr) - Returns the second component of the given expression.
If `expr` is a TIMESTAMP or a string that can be cast to timestamp,
it returns the second of that timestamp.
If `expr` is a nanosecond-precision timestamp TIMESTAMP_NTZ(p) or TIMESTAMP_LTZ(p)
with p in [7, 9] (since 4.3.0), it returns the second of that timestamp, ignoring the
sub-microsecond digits.
If `expr` is a TIME type (since 4.1.0), it returns the second of the time-of-day.

function.name: sentences
function.usage: sentences(str[, lang[, country]]) - Splits `str` into an array of array of words.

function.name: sequence
function.usage:
sequence(start, stop, step) - Generates an array of elements from start to stop (inclusive),
incrementing by step. The type of the returned elements is the same as the type of argument
expressions.
Supported types are: byte, short, integer, long, date, timestamp.
The start and stop expressions must resolve to the same type.
If start and stop expressions resolve to the 'date' or 'timestamp' type
then the step expression must resolve to the 'interval' or 'year-month interval' or
'day-time interval' type, otherwise to the same type as the start and stop expressions.

function.name: sha1
function.usage: sha1(expr) - Returns a sha1 hash value as a hex string of the `expr`.

function.name: sha
function.usage: sha(expr) - Returns a sha1 hash value as a hex string of the `expr`.

function.name: sha2
function.usage:
sha2(expr, bitLength) - Returns a checksum of SHA-2 family as a hex string of `expr`.
SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are supported. Bit length of 0 is equivalent to 256.

function.name: shiftleft
function.usage: base shiftleft exp - Bitwise left shift.

function.name: shiftright
function.usage: base shiftright expr - Bitwise (signed) right shift.

function.name: shiftrightunsigned
function.usage: base shiftrightunsigned expr - Bitwise unsigned right shift.

function.name: shuffle
function.usage: shuffle(array) - Returns a random permutation of the given array.

function.name: signum
function.usage: signum(expr) - Returns -1.0, 0.0 or 1.0 as `expr` is negative, 0 or positive.

function.name: sign
function.usage: sign(expr) - Returns -1.0, 0.0 or 1.0 as `expr` is negative, 0 or positive.

function.name: sin
function.usage: sin(expr) - Returns the sine of `expr`, as if computed by `java.lang.Math.sin`.

function.name: sinh
function.usage: sinh(expr) - Returns hyperbolic sine of `expr`, as if computed by `java.lang.Math.sinh`.

function.name: size
function.usage:
size(expr) - Returns the size of an array or a map.
This function returns -1 for null input only if spark.sql.ansi.enabled is false and
spark.sql.legacy.sizeOfNull is true. Otherwise, it returns null for null input.
With the default settings, the function returns null for null input.

function.name: cardinality
function.usage:
cardinality(expr) - Returns the size of an array or a map.
This function returns -1 for null input only if spark.sql.ansi.enabled is false and
spark.sql.legacy.sizeOfNull is true. Otherwise, it returns null for null input.
With the default settings, the function returns null for null input.

function.name: slice
function.usage: slice(a1, a2) - Returns true if a1 contains at least a non-null element present also in a2. If the arrays have no common element and they are both non-empty and either of them contains a null element null is returned, false otherwise.

function.name: sort_array
function.usage:
sort_array(array[, ascendingOrder]) - Sorts the input array in ascending or descending order
according to the natural ordering of the array elements. NaN is greater than any non-NaN
elements for double/float type. Null elements will be placed at the beginning of the returned
array in ascending order or at the end of the returned array in descending order.

function.name: soundex
function.usage: soundex(str) - Returns Soundex code of the string.

function.name: spark_partition_id
function.usage: spark_partition_id() - Returns the current partition id.

function.name: version
function.usage: version() - Returns the Spark version. The string contains 2 fields, the first being a release version and the second being a git revision.

function.name: sqrt
function.usage: sqrt(expr) - Returns the square root of `expr`.

function.name: stack
function.usage: stack(n, expr1, ..., exprk) - Separates `expr1`, ..., `exprk` into `n` rows. Uses column names col0, col1, etc. by default unless specified otherwise.

function.name: instr
function.usage:
instr(str, substr[, start[, occurrence]]) - Returns the (1-based) index of the specified
occurrence of `substr` in `str`, starting the search from position `start`.
If `start` is positive, the search proceeds forward;
if `start` is negative, the search proceeds backward.
`start` = 0 returns 0.
If `start` is not specified, it defaults to 1.
`occurrence` must be a positive integer and defaults to 1.

function.name: lpad
function.usage:
lpad(str, len[, pad]) - Returns `str`, left-padded with `pad` to a length of `len`.
If `str` is longer than `len`, the return value is shortened to `len` characters or bytes.
If `pad` is not specified, `str` will be padded to the left with space characters if it is
a character string, and with zeros if it is a byte sequence.

function.name: position
function.usage:
position(substr, str[, pos]) - Returns the position of the first occurrence of `substr` in `str` after position `pos`.
The given `pos` and return value are 1-based.

function.name: locate
function.usage:
locate(substr, str[, pos]) - Returns the position of the first occurrence of `substr` in `str` after position `pos`.
The given `pos` and return value are 1-based.

function.name: rpad
function.usage:
rpad(str, len[, pad]) - Returns `str`, right-padded with `pad` to a length of `len`.
If `str` is longer than `len`, the return value is shortened to `len` characters.
If `pad` is not specified, `str` will be padded to the right with space characters if it is
a character string, and with zeros if it is a binary string.

function.name: repeat
function.usage: repeat(str, n) - Returns the string which repeats the given string value n times.

function.name: replace
function.usage: replace(str, search[, replace]) - Replaces all occurrences of `search` with `replace`.

function.name: space
function.usage: space(n) - Returns a string consisting of `n` spaces.

function.name: split
function.usage: split(str, regex, limit) - Splits `str` around occurrences that match `regex`

function.name: str_to_map
function.usage: str_to_map(text[, pairDelim[, keyValueDelim]]) - Creates a map after splitting the text into key/value pairs using delimiters. Default delimiters are ',' for `pairDelim` and ':' for `keyValueDelim`. Both `pairDelim` and `keyValueDelim` are treated as regular expressions.

function.name: translate
function.usage: translate(input, from, to) - Translates the `input` string by replacing the characters present in the `from` string with the corresponding characters in the `to` string.

function.name: trim
function.usage:
trim(str) - Removes the leading and trailing space characters from `str`.
trim(BOTH FROM str) - Removes the leading and trailing space characters from `str`.
trim(LEADING FROM str) - Removes the leading space characters from `str`.
trim(TRAILING FROM str) - Removes the trailing space characters from `str`.
trim(trimStr FROM str) - Remove the leading and trailing `trimStr` characters from `str`.
trim(BOTH trimStr FROM str) - Remove the leading and trailing `trimStr` characters from `str`.
trim(LEADING trimStr FROM str) - Remove the leading `trimStr` characters from `str`.
trim(TRAILING trimStr FROM str) - Remove the trailing `trimStr` characters from `str`.

function.name: ltrim
function.usage: ltrim(str) - Removes the leading space characters from `str`.

function.name: rtrim
function.usage: rtrim(str) - Removes the trailing space characters from `str`.

function.name: to_csv
function.usage: to_csv(expr[, options]) - Returns a CSV string with a given struct value

function.name: to_json
function.usage: to_json(expr[, options]) - Returns a JSON string with a given struct value

function.name: substr
function.usage:
substr(str, pos[, len]) - Returns the substring of `str` that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`, or the slice of byte array that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`.
substr(str FROM pos[ FOR len]]) - Returns the substring of `str` that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`, or the slice of byte array that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`.

function.name: substring
function.usage:
substring(str, pos[, len]) - Returns the substring of `str` that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`, or the slice of byte array that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`.
substring(str FROM pos[ FOR len]]) - Returns the substring of `str` that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`, or the slice of byte array that starts at `pos` and is of length `len`.

function.name: substring_index
function.usage:
substring_index(str, delim, count) - Returns the substring from `str` before `count` occurrences of the delimiter `delim`.
If `count` is positive, everything to the left of the final delimiter (counting from the
left) is returned. If `count` is negative, everything to the right of the final delimiter
(counting from the right) is returned. The function substring_index performs a case-sensitive match
when searching for `delim`.
expr1 - expr2 - Returns `expr1`-`expr2`.

function.name: tan
function.usage: tan(expr) - Returns the tangent of `expr`, as if computed by `java.lang.Math.tan`.

function.name: tanh
function.usage:
tanh(expr) - Returns the hyperbolic tangent of `expr`, as if computed by
`java.lang.Math.tanh`.

function.name: window
function.example: SELECT a, window.start, window.end, count(*) as cnt FROM VALUES ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:00:00'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:04:30'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:06:00'), ('A2', '2021-01-01 00:01:00') AS tab(a, b) GROUP by a, window(b, '5 minutes') ORDER BY a, start
function.usage: window(time_column, window_duration[, slide_duration[, start_time]]) - Bucketize rows into one or more time windows given a timestamp specifying column. Window starts are inclusive but the window ends are exclusive, e.g. 12:05 will be in the window [12:05,12:10) but not in [12:00,12:05). Windows can support microsecond precision. Windows in the order of months are not supported. See 'Window Operations on Event Time' in Structured Streaming guide doc for detailed explanation and examples.

function.name: degrees
function.usage: degrees(expr) - Converts radians to degrees.

function.name: radians
function.usage: radians(expr) - Converts degrees to radians.

function.name: to_utc_timestamp
function.usage: to_utc_timestamp(timestamp, timezone) - Given a timestamp like '2017-07-14 02:40:00.0', interprets it as a time in the given time zone, and renders that time as a timestamp in UTC. For example, 'GMT+1' would yield '2017-07-14 01:40:00.0'.

function.name: to_unix_timestamp
function.usage: to_unix_timestamp(timeExp[, fmt]) - Returns the UNIX timestamp of the given time.

function.name: transform_keys
function.usage: transform_keys(expr, func) - Transforms elements in a map using the function.

function.name: transform_values
function.usage: transform_values(expr, func) - Transforms values in the map using the function.

function.name: trunc
function.usage: trunc(date, fmt) - Returns `date` with the time portion of the day truncated to the unit specified by the format model `fmt`.

function.name: date_trunc
function.usage: date_trunc(fmt, ts) - Returns timestamp `ts` truncated to the unit specified by the format model `fmt`.

function.name: typeof
function.usage: typeof(expr) - Return DDL-formatted type string for the data type of the input.

function.name: unbase64
function.usage: unbase64(str) - Converts the argument from a base 64 string `str` to a binary.

function.name: negative
function.usage: negative(expr) - Returns the negated value of `expr`.

function.name: positive
function.usage: positive(expr) - Returns the value of `expr`.

function.name: unhex
function.usage: unhex(expr) - Converts hexadecimal `expr` to binary.

function.name: unix_timestamp
function.usage: unix_timestamp([timeExp[, fmt]]) - Returns the UNIX timestamp of current or specified time.

function.name: ucase
function.usage: ucase(str) - Returns `str` with all characters changed to uppercase.

function.name: upper
function.usage: upper(str) - Returns `str` with all characters changed to uppercase.

function.name: uuid
function.usage: uuid() - Returns an universally unique identifier (UUID) string. The value is returned as a canonical UUID 36-character string.

function.name: weekday
function.usage: weekday(date) - Returns the day of the week for date/timestamp (0 = Monday, 1 = Tuesday, ..., 6 = Sunday).

function.name: weekofyear
function.usage: weekofyear(date) - Returns the week of the year of the given date. A week is considered to start on a Monday and week 1 is the first week with >3 days.

function.name: xxhash64
function.usage: xxhash64(expr1, expr2, ...) - Returns a 64-bit hash value of the arguments.

function.name: year
function.usage: year(date) - Returns the year component of the date/timestamp.

function.name: zip_with
function.usage: zip_with(left, right, func) - Merges the two given arrays, element-wise, into a single array using function. If one array is shorter, nulls are appended at the end to match the length of the longer array, before applying function.

function.name: approx_percentile
function.example: SELECT approx_percentile(col, array(0.5, 0.4, 0.1), 100) FROM VALUES (0), (1), (2), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
approx_percentile(col, percentage [, accuracy]) - Returns the approximate `percentile` of the numeric,
ansi interval or TIME column `col` which is the smallest value in the ordered `col` values (sorted
from least to greatest) such that no more than `percentage` of `col` values is less than
the value or equal to that value. The value of percentage must be between 0.0 and 1.0.
The `accuracy` parameter (default: 10000) is a positive numeric literal which controls
approximation accuracy at the cost of memory. Higher value of `accuracy` yields better
accuracy, `1.0/accuracy` is the relative error of the approximation.
When `percentage` is an array, each value of the percentage array must be between 0.0 and 1.0.
In this case, returns the approximate percentile array of column `col` at the given
percentage array.

function.name: percentile_approx
function.example: SELECT percentile_approx(col, array(0.5, 0.4, 0.1), 100) FROM VALUES (0), (1), (2), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
percentile_approx(col, percentage [, accuracy]) - Returns the approximate `percentile` of the numeric,
ansi interval or TIME column `col` which is the smallest value in the ordered `col` values (sorted
from least to greatest) such that no more than `percentage` of `col` values is less than
the value or equal to that value. The value of percentage must be between 0.0 and 1.0.
The `accuracy` parameter (default: 10000) is a positive numeric literal which controls
approximation accuracy at the cost of memory. Higher value of `accuracy` yields better
accuracy, `1.0/accuracy` is the relative error of the approximation.
When `percentage` is an array, each value of the percentage array must be between 0.0 and 1.0.
In this case, returns the approximate percentile array of column `col` at the given
percentage array.

function.name: avg
function.example: SELECT avg(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: avg(expr) - Returns the mean calculated from values of a group.

function.name: mean
function.example: SELECT mean(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: mean(expr) - Returns the mean calculated from values of a group.

function.name: bit_and
function.example: SELECT bit_and(col) FROM VALUES (3), (5) AS tab(col)
function.usage: bit_and(expr) - Returns the bitwise AND of all non-null input values, or null if none.

function.name: bit_or
function.example: SELECT bit_or(col) FROM VALUES (3), (5) AS tab(col)
function.usage: bit_or(expr) - Returns the bitwise OR of all non-null input values, or null if none.

function.name: bit_xor
function.example: SELECT bit_xor(col) FROM VALUES (3), (5) AS tab(col)
function.usage: bit_xor(expr) - Returns the bitwise XOR of all non-null input values, or null if none.

function.name: every

function.usage: every(expr) - Returns true if all values of `expr` are true.

function.name: bool_and

function.usage: bool_and(expr) - Returns true if all values of `expr` are true.

function.name: bool_or
function.example: SELECT bool_or(col) FROM VALUES (true), (false), (false) AS tab(col)
function.usage: bool_or(expr) - Returns true if at least one value of `expr` is true.

function.name: some
function.example: SELECT some(col) FROM VALUES (true), (false), (false) AS tab(col)
function.usage: some(expr) - Returns true if at least one value of `expr` is true.

function.name: any
function.example: SELECT any(col) FROM VALUES (true), (false), (false) AS tab(col)
function.usage: any(expr) - Returns true if at least one value of `expr` is true.

function.name: collect_list
function.example: SELECT collect_list(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (1) AS tab(col)
function.usage: collect_list(expr) - Collects and returns a list of non-unique elements.

function.name: collect_set
function.example: SELECT collect_set(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (1) AS tab(col)

function.name: corr
function.example: SELECT corr(c1, c2) FROM VALUES (3, 2), (3, 3), (6, 4) as tab(c1, c2)
function.usage: corr(expr1, expr2) - Returns Pearson coefficient of correlation between a set of number pairs.

function.name: count
function.example: SELECT count(*) FROM VALUES (NULL), (5), (5), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
count(*) - Returns the total number of retrieved rows, including rows containing null.
count(expr[, expr...]) - Returns the number of rows for which the supplied expression(s) are all non-null.
count(DISTINCT expr[, expr...]) - Returns the number of rows for which the supplied expression(s) are unique and non-null.

function.name: count_if
function.example: SELECT count_if(col % 2 = 0) FROM VALUES (NULL), (0), (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: count_if(expr) - Returns the number of `TRUE` values for the expression.

function.name: count_min_sketch
function.example: SELECT hex(count_min_sketch(col, 0.5d, 0.5d, 1)) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (1) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
count_min_sketch(col, eps, confidence, seed) - Returns a count-min sketch of a column with the given esp,
confidence and seed. The result is an array of bytes, which can be deserialized to a
`CountMinSketch` before usage. Count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure used for
cardinality estimation using sub-linear space.

function.name: covar_pop
function.example: SELECT covar_pop(c1, c2) FROM VALUES (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) AS tab(c1, c2)
function.usage: covar_pop(expr1, expr2) - Returns the population covariance of a set of number pairs.

function.name: covar_samp
function.example: SELECT covar_samp(c1, c2) FROM VALUES (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) AS tab(c1, c2)
function.usage: covar_samp(expr1, expr2) - Returns the sample covariance of a set of number pairs.

function.name: first_value
function.example: SELECT first_value(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
first_value(expr[, isIgnoreNull]) - Returns the first value of `expr` for a group of rows.
If `isIgnoreNull` is true, returns only non-null values.

function.name: first
function.example: SELECT first(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
first(expr[, isIgnoreNull]) - Returns the first value of `expr` for a group of rows.
If `isIgnoreNull` is true, returns only non-null values.

function.name: approx_count_distinct
function.usage:
approx_count_distinct(expr[, relativeSD]) - Returns the estimated cardinality by HyperLogLog++.
`relativeSD` defines the maximum relative standard deviation allowed.

function.name: kurtosis
function.example: SELECT kurtosis(col) FROM VALUES (-10), (-20), (100), (1000) AS tab(col)
function.usage: kurtosis(expr) - Returns the kurtosis value calculated from values of a group.

function.name: last_value
function.example: SELECT last_value(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
last_value(expr[, isIgnoreNull]) - Returns the last value of `expr` for a group of rows.
If `isIgnoreNull` is true, returns only non-null values

function.name: last
function.example: SELECT last(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
last(expr[, isIgnoreNull]) - Returns the last value of `expr` for a group of rows.
If `isIgnoreNull` is true, returns only non-null values

function.name: max
function.example: SELECT max(col) FROM VALUES (10), (50), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage: max(expr) - Returns the maximum value of `expr`.

function.name: max_by
function.example: SELECT max_by(x, y) FROM VALUES ('a', 10), ('b', 50), ('c', 20) AS tab(x, y)
function.usage:
max_by(x, y) - Returns the value of `x` associated with the maximum value of `y`.
max_by(x, y, k) - Returns an array of the `k` values of `x` associated with the
maximum values of `y`, sorted in descending order by `y`.
Returns NULL if there are no non-NULL ordering values.

function.name: min
function.example: SELECT min(col) FROM VALUES (10), (-1), (20) AS tab(col)
function.usage: min(expr) - Returns the minimum value of `expr`.

function.name: min_by
function.example: SELECT min_by(x, y) FROM VALUES ('a', 10), ('b', 50), ('c', 20) AS tab(x, y)
function.usage:
min_by(x, y) - Returns the value of `x` associated with the minimum value of `y`.
min_by(x, y, k) - Returns an array of the `k` values of `x` associated with the
minimum values of `y`, sorted in ascending order by `y`.
Returns NULL if there are no non-NULL ordering values.

function.name: percentile
function.example: SELECT percentile(col, 0.3) FROM VALUES (0), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
percentile(col, percentage [, frequency]) - Returns the exact percentile value of numeric,
ANSI interval or TIME column `col` at the given percentage. The value of percentage must be
between 0.0 and 1.0. The value of frequency should be positive integral
percentile(col, array(percentage1 [, percentage2]...) [, frequency]) - Returns the exact
percentile value array of numeric column `col` at the given percentage(s). Each value
of the percentage array must be between 0.0 and 1.0. The value of frequency should be
positive integral

function.name: skewness
function.example: SELECT skewness(col) FROM VALUES (-10), (-20), (100), (1000) AS tab(col)
function.usage: skewness(expr) - Returns the skewness value calculated from values of a group.

function.name: stddev_pop

function.usage: stddev_pop(expr) - Returns the population standard deviation calculated from values of a group.

function.name: stddev_samp
function.example: SELECT stddev_samp(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: stddev_samp(expr) - Returns the sample standard deviation calculated from values of a group.

function.name: stddev
function.example: SELECT stddev(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: stddev(expr) - Returns the sample standard deviation calculated from values of a group.

function.name: std
function.example: SELECT std(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: std(expr) - Returns the sample standard deviation calculated from values of a group.

function.name: sum
function.example: SELECT sum(col) FROM VALUES (5), (10), (15) AS tab(col)
function.usage: sum(expr) - Returns the sum calculated from values of a group.

function.name: var_pop
function.example: SELECT var_pop(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: var_pop(expr) - Returns the population variance calculated from values of a group.

function.name: var_samp
function.example: SELECT var_samp(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: var_samp(expr) - Returns the sample variance calculated from values of a group.

function.name: variance
function.example: SELECT variance(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (3) AS tab(col)
function.usage: variance(expr) - Returns the sample variance calculated from values of a group.

function.name: xpath_boolean
function.usage: xpath_boolean(xml, xpath) - Returns true if the XPath expression evaluates to true, or if a matching node is found.

function.name: xpath_number
function.usage: xpath_number(xml, xpath) - Returns a double value, the value zero if no match is found, or NaN if a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath_double
function.usage: xpath_double(xml, xpath) - Returns a double value, the value zero if no match is found, or NaN if a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath_float
function.usage: xpath_float(xml, xpath) - Returns a float value, the value zero if no match is found, or NaN if a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath_int
function.usage: xpath_int(xml, xpath) - Returns an integer value, or the value zero if no match is found, or a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath
function.usage: xpath(xml, xpath) - Returns a string array of values within the nodes of xml that match the XPath expression.

function.name: xpath_long
function.usage: xpath_long(xml, xpath) - Returns a long integer value, or the value zero if no match is found, or a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath_short
function.usage: xpath_short(xml, xpath) - Returns a short integer value, or the value zero if no match is found, or a match is found but the value is non-numeric.

function.name: xpath_string
function.usage: xpath_string(xml, xpath) - Returns the text contents of the first xml node that matches the XPath expression.

function.name: current_catalog
function.usage: current_catalog() - Returns the current catalog.

function.name: current_timezone
function.usage: current_timezone() - Returns the current session local timezone.

function.name: date_from_unix_date
function.usage: date_from_unix_date(days) - Create date from the number of days since 1970-01-01.

function.name: json_object_keys
function.usage: json_object_keys(json_object) - Returns all the keys of the outermost JSON object as an array.

function.name: json_array_length
function.usage: json_array_length(jsonArray) - Returns the number of elements in the outermost JSON array.

function.name: timestamp_micros
function.usage: timestamp_micros(microseconds) - Creates timestamp from the number of microseconds since UTC epoch.

function.name: timestamp_millis
function.usage: timestamp_millis(milliseconds) - Creates timestamp from the number of milliseconds since UTC epoch.

function.name: nth_value
function.example: SELECT a, b, nth_value(b, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) FROM VALUES ('A1', 2), ('A1', 1), ('A2', 3), ('A1', 1) tab(a, b)
function.usage:
nth_value(input[, offset]) - Returns the value of `input` at the row that is the `offset`th row
from beginning of the window frame. Offset starts at 1. If ignoreNulls=true, we will skip
nulls when finding the `offset`th row. Otherwise, every row counts for the `offset`. If
there is no such an `offset`th row (e.g., when the offset is 10, size of the window frame
is less than 10), null is returned.

function.name: raise_error
function.usage: raise_error( expr ) - Throws a USER_RAISED_EXCEPTION with `expr` as message.

function.name: rand
function.usage: rand([seed]) - Returns a random value with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) uniformly distributed values in [0, 1).

function.name: random
function.usage: random([seed]) - Returns a random value with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) uniformly distributed values in [0, 1).

function.name: randn
function.usage: randn([seed]) - Returns a random value with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) values drawn from the standard normal distribution.

function.name: regexp_extract_all
function.usage:
regexp_extract_all(str, regexp[, idx]) - Extract all strings in the `str` that match the `regexp`
expression and corresponding to the regex group index.

function.name: timestamp_seconds
function.usage: timestamp_seconds(seconds) - Creates timestamp from the number of seconds (can be fractional) since UTC epoch.

function.name: unix_date
function.usage: unix_date(date) - Returns the number of days since 1970-01-01.

function.name: unix_micros
function.usage: unix_micros(timestamp) - Returns the number of microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Truncates higher levels of precision.

function.name: unix_millis
function.usage: unix_millis(timestamp) - Returns the number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Truncates higher levels of precision.

function.name: unix_seconds

function.name: width_bucket
function.usage:
width_bucket(value, min_value, max_value, num_bucket) - Returns the bucket number to which
`value` would be assigned in an equiwidth histogram with `num_bucket` buckets,
in the range `min_value` to `max_value`."

function.name: bit_get
function.usage:
bit_get(expr, pos) - Returns the value of the bit (0 or 1) at the specified position.
The positions are numbered from right to left, starting at zero.
The position argument cannot be negative.

function.name: getbit
function.usage:
getbit(expr, pos) - Returns the value of the bit (0 or 1) at the specified position.
The positions are numbered from right to left, starting at zero.
The position argument cannot be negative.

function.name: current_user
function.usage: current_user() - user name of current execution context.

function.name: localtimestamp
function.usage:
localtimestamp() - Returns the current timestamp without time zone at the start of query evaluation. All calls of localtimestamp within the same query return the same value.
localtimestamp - Returns the current local date-time at the session time zone at the start of query evaluation.
localtimestamp(precision) - Returns the current local date-time with the given fractional-seconds precision. A precision in [7, 9] returns a nanosecond-precision TIMESTAMP_NTZ(precision) and requires spark.sql.timestampNanosTypes.enabled to be true; precision 6 returns the standard microsecond TIMESTAMP_NTZ.

function.name: make_dt_interval
function.usage: make_dt_interval([days[, hours[, mins[, secs]]]]) - Make DayTimeIntervalType duration from days, hours, mins and secs.

function.name: make_timestamp_ltz
function.usage:
make_timestamp_ltz(year, month, day, hour, min, sec[, timezone]) - Create the current timestamp with local time zone from year, month, day, hour, min, sec and (optional) timezone fields. If the configuration `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is false, the function returns NULL on invalid inputs. Otherwise, it will throw an error instead.
make_timestamp_ltz(date, time[, timezone]) - Create a local date-time from date, time and (optional) timezone fields.

function.name: make_timestamp_ntz
function.usage:
make_timestamp_ntz(year, month, day, hour, min, sec) - Create local date-time from year, month, day, hour, min, sec fields. If the configuration `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is false, the function returns NULL on invalid inputs. Otherwise, it will throw an error instead.
make_timestamp_ntz(date, time) - Create a local date-time from date and time fields.

function.name: make_ym_interval
function.usage: make_ym_interval([years[, months]]) - Make year-month interval from years, months.

function.name: to_timestamp_ltz
function.usage:
to_timestamp_ltz(timestamp_str[, fmt]) - Parses the `timestamp_str` expression with the `fmt` expression
to a timestamp with local time zone. Returns null with invalid input. By default, it follows casting rules to
a timestamp if the `fmt` is omitted.

function.name: to_timestamp_ntz
function.usage:
to_timestamp_ntz(timestamp_str[, fmt]) - Parses the `timestamp_str` expression with the `fmt` expression
to a timestamp without time zone. Returns null with invalid input. By default, it follows casting rules to
a timestamp if the `fmt` is omitted.

function.name: regexp
function.usage: regexp(str, regexp) - Returns true if `str` matches `regexp`, or false otherwise.

function.name: regexp_like
function.usage: regexp_like(str, regexp) - Returns true if `str` matches `regexp`, or false otherwise.

function.name: session_window
function.example: SELECT a, session_window.start, session_window.end, count(*) as cnt FROM VALUES ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:00:00'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:04:30'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:10:00'), ('A2', '2021-01-01 00:01:00') AS tab(a, b) GROUP by a, session_window(b, '5 minutes') ORDER BY a, start
function.usage: session_window(time_column, gap_duration) - Generates session window given a timestamp specifying column and gap duration. See 'Types of time windows' in Structured Streaming guide doc for detailed explanation and examples.

function.name: btrim
function.usage:
btrim(str) - Removes the leading and trailing space characters from `str`.
btrim(str, trimStr) - Remove the leading and trailing `trimStr` characters from `str`.

function.name: try_add
function.usage: try_add(expr1, expr2) - Returns the sum of `expr1`and `expr2` and the result is null on overflow.

function.name: try_divide
function.usage: try_divide(dividend, divisor) - Returns `dividend`/`divisor`. It always performs floating point division. Its result is always null if `expr2` is 0.

function.name: aes_decrypt
function.usage:
aes_decrypt(expr, key[, mode[, padding[, aad]]]) - Returns a decrypted value of `expr` using AES in `mode` with `padding`.
Key lengths of 16, 24 and 32 bits are supported. Supported combinations of (`mode`, `padding`) are ('ECB', 'PKCS'), ('GCM', 'NONE') and ('CBC', 'PKCS').
Optional additional authenticated data (AAD) is only supported for GCM. If provided for encryption, the identical AAD value must be provided for decryption.
The default mode is GCM.

function.name: aes_encrypt
function.usage:
aes_encrypt(expr, key[, mode[, padding[, iv[, aad]]]]) - Returns an encrypted value of `expr` using AES in given `mode` with the specified `padding`.
Key lengths of 16, 24 and 32 bits are supported. Supported combinations of (`mode`, `padding`) are ('ECB', 'PKCS'), ('GCM', 'NONE') and ('CBC', 'PKCS').
Optional initialization vectors (IVs) are only supported for CBC and GCM modes. These must be 16 bytes for CBC and 12 bytes for GCM. If not provided, a random vector will be generated and prepended to the output.
Optional additional authenticated data (AAD) is only supported for GCM. If provided for encryption, the identical AAD value must be provided for decryption.
The default mode is GCM.

function.name: array_size
function.usage: array_size(expr) - Returns the size of an array. The function returns null for null input.

function.name: contains
function.usage:
contains(left, right) - Returns a boolean. The value is True if right is found inside left.
Returns NULL if either input expression is NULL. Otherwise, returns False.
Both left or right must be of STRING or BINARY type.

function.name: convert_timezone

function.name: endswith

Both left or right must be of STRING or BINARY type.

function.name: ilike

function.name: split_part

split_part(str, delimiter, partNum) - Splits `str` by delimiter and return
requested part of the split (1-based). If any input is null, returns null.
if `partNum` is out of range of split parts, returns empty string. If `partNum` is 0,
throws an error. If `partNum` is negative, the parts are counted backward from the

startswith(left, right) - Returns a boolean. The value is True if left starts with right.
Returns NULL if either input expression is NULL. Otherwise, returns False.
Both left or right must be of STRING or BINARY type.

function.name: to_binary
function.usage:
to_binary(str[, fmt]) - Converts the input `str` to a binary value based on the supplied `fmt`.
`fmt` can be a case-insensitive string literal of "hex", "utf-8", "utf8", or "base64".
By default, the binary format for conversion is "hex" if `fmt` is omitted.
The function returns NULL if at least one of the input parameters is NULL.

function.name: to_number
function.usage:
to_number(expr, fmt) - Convert string 'expr' to a number based on the string format 'fmt'.
Throws an exception if the conversion fails. The format can consist of the following
characters, case insensitive:
'0' or '9': Specifies an expected digit between 0 and 9. A sequence of 0 or 9 in the format
string matches a sequence of digits in the input string. If the 0/9 sequence starts with
0 and is before the decimal point, it can only match a digit sequence of the same size.
Otherwise, if the sequence starts with 9 or is after the decimal point, it can match a
digit sequence that has the same or smaller size.
'.' or 'D': Specifies the position of the decimal point (optional, only allowed once).
',' or 'G': Specifies the position of the grouping (thousands) separator (,). There must be
a 0 or 9 to the left and right of each grouping separator. 'expr' must match the
grouping separator relevant for the size of the number.
'$': Specifies the location of the $ currency sign. This character may only be specified
once.
'S' or 'MI': Specifies the position of a '-' or '+' sign (optional, only allowed once at
the beginning or end of the format string). Note that 'S' allows '-' but 'MI' does not.
'PR': Only allowed at the end of the format string; specifies that 'expr' indicates a
negative number with wrapping angled brackets.
('<1>').

function.name: try_element_at
function.usage:
try_element_at(array, index) - Returns element of array at given (1-based) index. If Index is 0,
Spark will throw an error. If index < 0, accesses elements from the last to the first.
The function always returns NULL if the index exceeds the length of the array.
try_element_at(map, key) - Returns value for given key. The function always returns NULL
if the key is not contained in the map.

function.name: try_multiply

function.name: try_to_binary
function.usage: try_to_binary(str[, fmt]) - This is a special version of `to_binary` that performs the same operation, but returns a NULL value instead of raising an error if the conversion cannot be performed.

function.name: try_to_number
function.usage:
try_to_number(expr, fmt) - Convert string 'expr' to a number based on the string format `fmt`.
Returns NULL if the string 'expr' does not match the expected format. The format follows the
same semantics as the to_number function.

function.name: array_agg
function.example: SELECT array_agg(col) FROM VALUES (1), (2), (1) AS tab(col)
function.usage: array_agg(expr) - Collects and returns a list of non-unique elements.

function.name: histogram_numeric
function.example: SELECT histogram_numeric(col, 5) FROM VALUES (0), (1), (2), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
histogram_numeric(expr, nb) - Computes a histogram on numeric 'expr' using nb bins.
The return value is an array of (x,y) pairs representing the centers of the
histogram's bins. As the value of 'nb' is increased, the histogram approximation
gets finer-grained, but may yield artifacts around outliers. In practice, 20-40
histogram bins appear to work well, with more bins being required for skewed or
smaller datasets. Note that this function creates a histogram with non-uniform
bin widths. It offers no guarantees in terms of the mean-squared-error of the
histogram, but in practice is comparable to the histograms produced by the R/S-Plus
statistical computing packages. Note: the output type of the 'x' field in the return value is
propagated from the input value consumed in the aggregate function.

function.usage: regr_avgx(y, x) - Returns the average of the independent variable for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.usage: regr_avgy(y, x) - Returns the average of the dependent variable for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: regr_r2

function.name: array_append

array_append(array, element) - Add the element at the end of the array passed as first
argument. Type of element should be similar to type of the elements of the array.
Null element is also appended into the array. But if the array passed, is NULL
output is NULL

function.name: array_compact

function.name: array_insert

Array indices start at 1. The maximum negative index is -1 for which the function inserts
new element after the current last element.
Index above array size appends the array, or prepends the array if index is negative,
with 'null' elements.

function.name: current_schema

function.name: user

function.name: dateadd

function.name: equal_null

but returns true if both are null, false if one of the them is null.

function.name: mask

mask(input[, upperChar, lowerChar, digitChar, otherChar]) - masks the given string value.
The function replaces characters with 'X' or 'x', and numbers with 'n'.
This can be useful for creating copies of tables with sensitive information removed.

function.name: regexp_count
function.example: SELECT regexp_count('Steven Jones and Stephen Smith are the best players', 'Ste(v|ph)en')
function.usage: regexp_count(str, regexp) - Returns a count of the number of times that the regular expression pattern `regexp` is matched in the string `str`.

function.name: regexp_instr
function.usage: regexp_instr(str, regexp) - Searches a string for a regular expression and returns an integer that indicates the beginning position of the matched substring. Positions are 1-based, not 0-based. If no match is found, returns 0.

function.name: regexp_substr
function.example: SELECT regexp_substr('Steven Jones and Stephen Smith are the best players', 'Ste(v|ph)en')
function.usage: regexp_substr(str, regexp) - Returns the substring that matches the regular expression `regexp` within the string `str`. If the regular expression is not found, the result is null.

function.name: to_char
function.usage: to_char(expr, format) - Convert `expr` to a string based on the `format`. Throws an exception if the conversion fails. The format can consist of the following characters, case insensitive: '0' or '9': Specifies an expected digit between 0 and 9. A sequence of 0 or 9 in the format string matches a sequence of digits in the input value, generating a result string of the same length as the corresponding sequence in the format string. The result string is left-padded with zeros if the 0/9 sequence comprises more digits than the matching part of the decimal value, starts with 0, and is before the decimal point. Otherwise, it is padded with spaces. '.' or 'D': Specifies the position of the decimal point (optional, only allowed once). ',' or 'G': Specifies the position of the grouping (thousands) separator (,). There must be a 0 or 9 to the left and right of each grouping separator. '$': Specifies the location of the $ currency sign. This character may only be specified once. 'S' or 'MI': Specifies the position of a '-' or '+' sign (optional, only allowed once at the beginning or end of the format string). Note that 'S' prints '+' for positive values but 'MI' prints a space. 'PR': Only allowed at the end of the format string; specifies that the result string will be wrapped by angle brackets if the input value is negative. ('<1>'). If `expr` is a datetime, `format` shall be a valid datetime pattern, see Datetime Patterns. If `expr` is a binary, it is converted to a string in one of the formats: 'base64': a base 64 string. 'hex': a string in the hexadecimal format. 'utf-8': the input binary is decoded to UTF-8 string.

function.name: try_to_timestamp
function.usage:
try_to_timestamp(timestamp_str[, fmt]) - Parses the `timestamp_str` expression with the `fmt` expression
to a timestamp. The function always returns null on an invalid input with/without ANSI SQL
mode enabled. By default, it follows casting rules to a timestamp if the `fmt` is omitted.
The result data type is consistent with the value of configuration `spark.sql.timestampType`.

function.name: url_decode

function.name: url_encode
function.usage: url_encode(str) - Translates a string into 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' format using a specific encoding scheme.

function.name: window_time
function.example: SELECT a, window.start as start, window.end as end, window_time(window), cnt FROM (SELECT a, window, count(*) as cnt FROM VALUES ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:00:00'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:04:30'), ('A1', '2021-01-01 00:06:00'), ('A2', '2021-01-01 00:01:00') AS tab(a, b) GROUP by a, window(b, '5 minutes') ORDER BY a, window.start)
function.usage: window_time(window_column) - Extract the time value from time/session window column which can be used for event time value of window. The extracted time is (window.end - 1) which reflects the fact that the aggregating windows have exclusive upper bound - [start, end) See 'Window Operations on Event Time' in Structured Streaming guide doc for detailed explanation and examples.

function.name: any_value
function.example: SELECT any_value(col) FROM VALUES (10), (5), (20) AS tab(col)

any_value(expr[, isIgnoreNull]) - Returns some value of `expr` for a group of rows.
If `isIgnoreNull` is true, returns only non-null values.

function.name: median
function.example: SELECT median(col) FROM VALUES (0), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage: median(col) - Returns the median of numeric, ANSI interval or TIME column `col`.

function.name: mode
function.example: SELECT mode(col) FROM VALUES (0), (10), (10) AS tab(col)
function.usage:
mode(col[, deterministic]) - Returns the most frequent value for the values within `col`. NULL values are ignored. If all the values are NULL, or there are 0 rows, returns NULL.
When multiple values have the same greatest frequency then either any of values is returned if `deterministic` is false or is not defined, or the lowest value is returned if `deterministic` is true.
mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) - Returns the most frequent value for the values within `col` (specified in ORDER BY clause). NULL values are ignored.
If all the values are NULL, or there are 0 rows, returns NULL. When multiple values have the same greatest frequency only one value will be returned.
The value will be chosen based on sort direction. Return the smallest value if sort direction is asc or the largest value if sort direction is desc from multiple values with the same frequency.

function.usage: regr_intercept(y, x) - Returns the intercept of the univariate linear regression line for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: regr_sxx
function.example: SELECT regr_sxx(y, x) FROM VALUES (1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4) AS tab(y, x)
function.usage: regr_sxx(y, x) - Returns REGR_COUNT(y, x) * VAR_POP(x) for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: regr_sxy
function.example: SELECT regr_sxy(y, x) FROM VALUES (1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4) AS tab(y, x)
function.usage: regr_sxy(y, x) - Returns REGR_COUNT(y, x) * COVAR_POP(y, x) for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: regr_syy
function.example: SELECT regr_syy(y, x) FROM VALUES (1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4) AS tab(y, x)
function.usage: regr_syy(y, x) - Returns REGR_COUNT(y, x) * VAR_POP(y) for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: regr_slope
function.example: SELECT regr_slope(y, x) FROM VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4) AS tab(y, x)
function.usage: regr_slope(y, x) - Returns the slope of the linear regression line for non-null pairs in a group, where `y` is the dependent variable and `x` is the independent variable.

function.name: to_varchar

A sequence of 0 or 9 in the format string matches a sequence of digits in the input value, generating a result string of the same length as the corresponding sequence in the format string. The result string is left-padded with zeros if the 0/9 sequence comprises more digits than the matching part of the decimal value, starts with 0, and is before the decimal point. ',' or 'G': Specifies the position of the grouping (thousands) separator (,). There must be a 0 or 9 to the left and right of each grouping separator. '$': Specifies the location of the $ currency sign. This character may only be specified once. 'S' or 'MI': Specifies the position of a '-' or '+' sign (optional, only allowed once at the beginning or end of the format string). Note that 'S' prints '+' for positive values but 'MI' prints a space. 'PR': Only allowed at the end of the format string; specifies that the result string will be wrapped by angle brackets if the input value is negative. ('<1>'). If k is not specified, the merged sketch adopts the k value from the first input sketch.

function.name: tuple_intersection_agg_double
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_double(tuple_intersection_agg_double(sketch)) FROM (SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (1, 5.0D), (2, 10.0D), (3, 15.0D) tab(key, summary) UNION ALL SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (2, 3.0D), (3, 7.0D), (4, 12.0D) tab(key, summary))
function.usage:
tuple_intersection_agg_double(child, mode) - Returns the intersected TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`child` should be a binary TupleSketch representation created with a double type summary.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries during intersection (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: tuple_intersection_agg_integer
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_integer(tuple_intersection_agg_integer(sketch)) FROM (SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) tab(key, summary) UNION ALL SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4) tab(key, summary))
function.usage:
tuple_intersection_agg_integer(child, mode) - Returns the intersected TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`child` should be a binary TupleSketch representation created with an integer type summary.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries during intersection (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: tuple_sketch_agg_double
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_double(tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary, 12, 'sum')) FROM VALUES (1, 5.0D), (1, 1.0D), (2, 2.0D), (2, 3.0D), (3, 2.2D) tab(key, summary)
function.usage:
tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary, lgNomEntries, mode) - Returns the TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`key` is the expression for unique value counting.
`summary` is the double value to be aggregated.
`lgNomEntries` is the log-base-2 of nominal entries, with nominal entries deciding
the number buckets or slots for the TupleSketch. Default is 12.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: tuple_sketch_agg_integer
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_integer(tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary, 12, 'sum')) FROM VALUES (1, 5), (1, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2) tab(key, summary)
function.usage:
tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary, lgNomEntries, mode) - Returns the TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`key` is the expression for unique value counting.
`summary` is the integer value to be aggregated.
`lgNomEntries` is the log-base-2 of nominal entries, with nominal entries deciding
the number buckets or slots for the TupleSketch. Default is 12.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: tuple_union_agg_double
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_double(tuple_union_agg_double(sketch)) FROM (SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (1, 5.0D), (2, 10.0D) tab(key, summary) UNION ALL SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_double(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (2, 3.0D), (3, 7.0D) tab(key, summary))
function.usage:
tuple_union_agg_double(child, lgNomEntries, mode) - Returns the unioned TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`child` should be a binary TupleSketch representation created with a double type summary.
`lgNomEntries` is the log-base-2 of nominal entries for the union operation. Default is 12.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries during union (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: tuple_union_agg_integer
function.example: SELECT tuple_sketch_estimate_integer(tuple_union_agg_integer(sketch)) FROM (SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (1, 5), (2, 10) tab(key, summary) UNION ALL SELECT tuple_sketch_agg_integer(key, summary) as sketch FROM VALUES (2, 3), (3, 7) tab(key, summary))
function.usage:
tuple_union_agg_integer(child, lgNomEntries, mode) - Returns the unioned TupleSketch compact binary representation.
`child` should be a binary TupleSketch representation created with an integer type summary.
`lgNomEntries` is the log-base-2 of nominal entries for the union operation. Default is 12.
`mode` is the aggregation mode for numeric summaries during union (sum, min, max, alwaysone). Default is sum.

function.name: is_valid_variant
function.usage: is_valid_variant(v) - Returns true if the variant is valid, false if it is malformed,

function.name: to_base32
function.usage: to_base32(bin) - Converts the argument from a binary `bin` to a base 32 string.

function.name: counter_diff
function.example: SELECT m, t, c, counter_diff(c) OVER (PARTITION BY m ORDER BY t) AS diff FROM VALUES ('http_requests', TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00', 100), ('http_requests', TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:01:00', 200), ('http_requests', TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:02:00', 400), ('http_requests', TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:03:00', 50), ('http_requests', TIMESTAMP_NTZ '2026-01-01 00:04:00', 100) AS tab(m, t, c) ORDER BY t
function.usage:
counter_diff(value [, start_time]) - Computes the differences between consecutive cumulative counter
values in a time series, thereby converting the counter from the cumulative to the delta
format.

function.name: localtime
function.usage:
localtime([precision]) - Returns the current time at the start of query evaluation.
All calls of current_time within the same query return the same value.
localtime - Returns the current time at the start of query evaluation.

function.name: hmac
function.usage: hmac(key, message[, algorithm]) - Returns the keyed-hash message authentication code (HMAC) of `message` using `key` and the hash `algorithm`. The result is returned as raw MAC bytes; wrap it with `hex` or `base64` for a textual value. The default algorithm is 'SHA-256'.

function.name: jaro_winkler_similarity
function.usage: jaro_winkler_similarity(str1, str2) - Returns the Jaro-Winkler similarity between the two given strings. The result is a double between 0 and 1, where 1 means identical.

function.name: timestamp_nanos
function.usage: timestamp_nanos(nanoseconds) - Creates timestamp with the local time zone and nanosecond precision (TIMESTAMP_LTZ(9)) from the number of nanoseconds since UTC epoch.

function.name: from_base32
function.usage: from_base32(str) - Converts the argument from a base 32 string `str` to a binary.

function.name: unix_nanos
function.usage: unix_nanos(timestamp) - Returns the number of nanoseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

function.name: collect_union
function.example: SELECT collect_union(col) FROM VALUES (array(1, 2)), (array(2, 3)), (array(1)) AS tab(col)
function.usage: collect_union(expr) - Collects and returns a set of unique elements.

config.name: spark.deploy.zookeeper.url
config.doc: When `${RECOVERY_MODE.key}` is set to ZOOKEEPER, this configuration is used to set the zookeeper URL to connect to.

config.name: spark.history.fs.logDirectory
